messages.subject: Fitting Homogenous Markov Model
parts:
Hello,

I am trying to use a multinomial likelihood to fit an HMM.

my data are organized as
vector [3] State [Ntime];

and I am trying to code the likelihood as follows

for(tm in 2:Ntime){
theta[tm]<-Prob*State[tm-1];
State[tm]~multinomial(theta[tm]);
}


I get the following error
DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
no matches for function name="multinomial_log"
    arg 0 type=vector
    arg 1 type=vector
available function signatures for multinomial_log:
0.  multinomial_log(int[1], vector) : real
unknown distribution=multinomial
Parser expecting: <eps>

I understand that I am incorrectly using variable types, and that is why the multinomial likelihood is not working. I have been playing with the code for a while, and am at a loss as to how to make it work.

I was hoping someone could please suggest how to make this work?

thank you

mark

This is saying that the multinomial distribution is expecting an integer array for the first argument (or left of the twiddle) and a vector for the second. It is also telling you that multinomial_log is actually called with vector, vector.  For this to work, State needs to be declared as "int State[Ntime, 3]",  I think.

I understand that I am incorrectly using variable types, and that is why the multinomial likelihood is not working. I have been playing with the code for a while, and am at a loss as to how to make it work.

I was hoping someone could please suggest how to make this work?

thank you

mark

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Fitting Homogenous Markov Model
parts:
To answer your literal question: You can assign individual int
values to real variables. So you could define a matrix and then
assign it:

int foo[I,J];
matrix[I,J] bar;
for (i in 1:I)
for (j in 1:J)
bar[i,j] <- foo[i,j];

But I somehow doubt this is what you want to be doing anyway.
Why would you multiply probabilities by states in an HMM
implementation?

Don't worry about bothering us with questions. Well, maybe
a little bit --- we don't have infinite amounts of time. But
it's important for us to hear where people are getting confused.
And we'd rather help than just frustrate our users. And then
hopefully make things clearer.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Fitting Homogenous Markov Model
parts:
It's helpful for us to see the whole model.
It's hard to make recommendations based on model fragments.
More below.

On Jun 14, 2014, at 7:08 PM, Markian Pahuta <mark....@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> OK, thank you. Perhaps i'll explain what I am trying to do. I have this model working in JAGS with dmstate but would like to move to Stan.
>
> My observed variable is a patient's health state (healthy, ill or dead). I would like to estimate the transition intensity matrix.
>
> I think I should be using the following likelihood
> for(tm in 2:Ntime){
> State[tm]~multinomial(TransMatrix * State[tm-1]);
>
> }
>

Stan has both a categorical distribution and a multinomial,
and you almost certainly want the categorical for this (single integer
outcome) and not the multinomial (vector of counts outcome).

Look at the signatures in the index of the manual and then look at
the definitions to make sure you're using the right distribution.

> Where state is a integer vector, TransMatrix is a 3x3 matrix... but then what do I do about State[tm-1].... I can't do integer by matrix multiplication. Should I have 2 variables for state, one integer and one vector? or is there a trick I could use with the categorical distribution? Really hoping for some advice.

Yes, you need to either do the matrix multiplication by hand in a loop,
or assign the integer values to a matrix and then use matrix multiplication.

I still don't understand why you'd want to matrix multiply states,
but I thought I'd at least answer your literal question.

- Bob

messages.author: 368f61d9252655a2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Fitting Homogenous Markov Model
parts:
Is the goal of that matrix multiplication just to get the transition probabilities corresponding to previsious State? For example, if State[tm-1]==2, you would like to get row number 2 from TransMatrix? The problem is that it actually return column 2, I can't see how that could be what you want.

That being said, I think it would be much cleaner to use categorical distribution directly instead of multinomial. But it requires a couple of changes to the original code. The main thing is that instead of of representing the State as a vector of length three we use just integers (ie. State==1 or State==2 or State==3).

I have attached edited version of the model to this post. In addition of that change of the distribution, I added parameter TAU to the parameter list (and give it a prior distribution) and changed the data generation accordingly. Did you want to have 5 patients&52 datapoints or just one? If more than one, change the State to integer array etc.

Edit: Didn't noticed at first, but the transformed parameters part of the model doesn't always produce matrix with row sums of exactly 1. Is there any particular reason to use that particular parametrization, or would it be possible to use something else, like softmax?

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Fitting Homogenous Markov Model
parts:
The most efficient thing to use for a single draw is
categorical_logit. Unfortunately, that has a memory leak
in Stan 2.2 that's fixed for 2.3, which should be out soon.

Until then, I'd suggest just using exp(alpha) / sum(alpha)
to implement softmax and plug into the categorical distribution.

And when you say it's slow, I'm curious how it compares to JAGS
in terms of convergence and mixing speed (wall time to convergence
and number of effective samples per time unit after convergence).
(Just counting iterations isn't useful to compare different MCMC
algorithms.)

- Bob

On Jun 16, 2014, at 12:18 AM, Markian Pahuta <mark....@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi

> I will try to formally compare the two and post to the board
>
> Alpha should be my computed transition probabilities with rounding error?

No --- alpha should be the regression values on the unconstrained
scale.

softmax(alpha) =def= exp(alpha) / sum(exp(alpha))

Sorry --- I missed the exp(alpha) on the first one.

So you want to do this with a local variable for exp(alpha), as in:

vector[K] alpha;

{
vector[K] exp_alpha;
simplex[K] softmax_alpha;
exp_alpha <- exp(alpha);
softmax_alpha <- exp_alpha / sum(exp_alpha);
... use softmax_alpha ...
}

Using the brackets will make exp_alpha and softmax_alpha local
variables. If you want to save softmax_alpha, declare it as
a transformed parameter.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Fitting Homogenous Markov Model
parts:
softmax is the inverse link function for multi-logistic
GLMs.

softmax maps arbitrary points alpha in R^K into K-simplexes
(i.e., K-vectors with non-negative vectors that sum to 1).
A K-simplex is the parameter to a categorical (or multinomial)
distribution. It's also the support for a K-dimensional Dirichlet
distribution.

I don't know what a "transition intensity" is.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Fitting Homogenous Markov Model
parts:
Nope --- I'm afraid that's not what it is.
If you want to implement what's in that Wikipedia page, you'll
have to do it by hand.

I was confusing what you were doing with a discrete time
HMM. I know nothing about the continuous versions.

If they're useful, then it might make sense to build some of
this into Stan. I've been thinking it'd be nice to have some
built-in support for some of our models that can be coded, but
are complex, such as:

* mixtures

* (discrete) hidden Markov models (HMM)

* generalized linear models (GLM)

* Gaussian processes (GP)

All of these things use built-ins wrapped into larger structures.
Functions may help implement some of this more quickly when we can
supply a library easily.

- Bob

On Jun 16, 2014, at 2:35 AM, Markian Pahuta <mark....@gmail.com> wrote:

> By transition intensity I mean the individual elements of what this wiki article calls the Q matrix (http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous-time_Markov_chain)
>
> On Sunday, June 15, 2014 7:55:36 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> softmax is the inverse link function for multi-logistic
> GLMs.
>
> softmax maps arbitrary points alpha in R^K into K-simplexes
> (i.e., K-vectors with non-negative vectors that sum to 1).
> A K-simplex is the parameter to a categorical (or multinomial)
> distribution. It's also the support for a K-dimensional Dirichlet
> distribution.
>
> I don't know what a "transition intensity" is.
>
> - Bob
>
> On Jun 16, 2014, at 12:39 AM, Markian Pahuta <mark....@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > sorry for all the questions, im not familiar with softmax.
> >
> > i am specifically interested in regression on transition intensities. the parameter estimates using softmax wont have the same interpretation as with transition intensities will they?
> >
> >
> > On Sun, Jun 15, 2014 at 7:33 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >
> > On Jun 16, 2014, at 12:18 AM, Markian Pahuta <mark....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > > Hi
> > >
> > > I will try to formally compare the two and post to the board
> > >
> > > Alpha should be my computed transition probabilities with rounding error?
> >
> > No --- alpha should be the regression values on the unconstrained
> > scale.
> >
> > softmax(alpha) =def= exp(alpha) / sum(exp(alpha))
> >
> > Sorry --- I missed the exp(alpha) on the first one.
> >
> > So you want to do this with a local variable for exp(alpha), as in:
> >
> > vector[K] alpha;
> >
> > {
> > vector[K] exp_alpha;
> > simplex[K] softmax_alpha;
> > exp_alpha <- exp(alpha);
> > softmax_alpha <- exp_alpha / sum(exp_alpha);
> > ... use softmax_alpha ...
> > }
> >
> > Using the brackets will make exp_alpha and softmax_alpha local
> > variables. If you want to save softmax_alpha, declare it as
> > a transformed parameter.
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> > >
> > > On Jun 15, 2014 7:09 PM, "Bob Carpenter" <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > > The most efficient thing to use for a single draw is
> > > categorical_logit. Unfortunately, that has a memory leak
> > > in Stan 2.2 that's fixed for 2.3, which should be out soon.
> > >
> > > Until then, I'd suggest just using exp(alpha) / sum(alpha)
> > > to implement softmax and plug into the categorical distribution.
> > >
> > > And when you say it's slow, I'm curious how it compares to JAGS
> > > in terms of convergence and mixing speed (wall time to convergence
> > > and number of effective samples per time unit after convergence).
> > > (Just counting iterations isn't useful to compare different MCMC
> > > algorithms.)
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > > On Jun 15, 2014, at 2:18 PM, Markian Pahuta <mark....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > > Hi Everyone,
> > > >
> > > > Thank you for your help.
> > > >
> > > > I have re-worked my code using all of your suggestions. It is attached and works correctly. I have expanded it to the full hierarchical model: level 1 = patient, level 2 = study. I have added in the random effects.
> > > >
> > > > I am a little unclear on how to use softmax wrt transition probabilities. In JAGS, I modeled transition intensities as a GLM and then recovered the transition probability matrix using the matrix exponential. My understanding is that I can't do this in Stan. So instead I have hard-coded the calculation of transition probabilities (rows 30-58). I think due to rounding error, transition probabilities do not add to 1. How would I go about using softmax for this? Or could I use another strategy?
> > > >
> > > > Also, if anyone has efficiency suggestion for the code it would be greatly appreciated, it runs quite slow.
> > > >
> > > > Again thanks for all of the help!
> > > >
> > > > Mark
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Saturday, June 14, 2014 4:31:28 PM UTC-4, Herra Huu wrote:
> > > > Is the goal of that matrix multiplication just to get the transition probabilities corresponding to previsious State? For example, if State[tm-1]==2, you would like to get row number 2 from TransMatrix? The problem is that it actually return column 2, I can't see how that could be what you want.
> > > >
> > > > That being said, I think it would be much cleaner to use categorical distribution directly instead of multinomial. But it requires a couple of changes to the original code. The main thing is that instead of of representing the State as a vector of length three we use just integers (ie. State==1 or State==2 or State==3).
> > > >
> > > > I have attached edited version of the model to this post. In addition of that change of the distribution, I added parameter TAU to the parameter list (and give it a prior distribution) and changed the data generation accordingly. Did you want to have 5 patients&52 datapoints or just one? If more than one, change the State to integer array etc.
> > > >
> > > > Edit: Didn't noticed at first, but the transformed parameters part of the model doesn't always produce matrix with row sums of exactly 1. Is there any particular reason to use that particular parametrization, or would it be possible to use something else, like softmax?
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On Saturday, June 14, 2014 9:08:57 PM UTC+3, Markian Pahuta wrote:
> > > >
> > > > My observed variable is a patient's health state (healthy, ill or dead). I would like to estimate the transition intensity matrix.
> > > >
> > > > I think I should be using the following likelihood
> > > > for(tm in 2:Ntime){
> > > > State[tm]~multinomial(TransMatrix * State[tm-1]);
> > > >
> > > > }
> > > >
